paragraphs: AgentLAB examines security failures that develop across extended interactions between a user, an agent, and its environment. These attacks can pursue objectives that are infeasible within a single exchange. The paper therefore treats the full interaction sequence as the unit of evaluation, reflecting how agents operate while solving complex tasks.

The benchmark covers five attack types: intent hijacking, tool chaining, task injection, objective drifting, and memory poisoning. It contains 644 security test cases across 28 realistic agent environments. This breadth lets researchers evaluate several ways an adversary can exploit an agent over time, including changes to its objectives and stored information.

Evaluations of representative agents find substantial susceptibility to these adaptive attacks. Defenses developed for single-turn interactions also fail to reliably mitigate the longer attacks. The findings show why performance on isolated safety checks provides an incomplete assessment of agent security. AgentLAB supplies a common evaluation framework for measuring whether future defenses remain effective throughout an extended task.
icml-2026-agentlab-benchmarking-llm-agen.tldr: AgentLAB tests attacks that unfold across extended agent interactions and finds that evaluated agents and single-turn defenses remain vulnerable.

paragraphs: TRACED evaluates language-model reasoning by examining the geometry of a reasoning trace. A single probability score can miss how reasoning develops along the way. The paper instead asks whether the trace makes sustained progress and whether its path remains stable, treating these as complementary signals of reasoning quality.

The framework measures progress through displacement and stability through curvature. The authors identify a separation in which correct reasoning follows trajectories with substantial progress and relatively stable movement, while hallucinations show stalled progress and fluctuating curvature. They interpret high curvature as hesitation loops and displacement as accumulating certainty, connecting the geometric measurements to recognizable reasoning behaviors.

These signals feed into a probabilistic framework that reports competitive performance and superior robustness across diverse benchmarks. The contribution is both evaluative and interpretive: the geometry helps assess reliability while describing how a trace proceeds or gets stuck. The reported patterns support this approach to understanding reasoning dynamics without reducing the entire process to one confidence value.
icml-2026-beyond-scalars-evaluating-and-.tldr: TRACED uses geometric progress and stability in reasoning traces to assess reliability and interpret patterns associated with correct reasoning and hallucinations.

paragraphs: A world model helps a reinforcement-learning agent learn how its environment behaves. The paper describes a tension between accurately modeling environmental dynamics and emphasizing the features that matter for decisions. Models optimized for likelihood can overlook task relevance, while approaches focused on value can deliver suboptimal performance.

The proposed Value-Aligned World Model combines these priorities through a regularization term inside the model’s latent representation. This term encourages attention to task-relevant features while preserving the structure of stochastic dynamics. An adaptive weighting mechanism adjusts the balance between reconstruction fidelity and decision usefulness, functioning as a curriculum that regulates itself during optimization.

Experiments on Atari 100k and DeepMind Control show consistent improvements to existing methods, with minimal additional code and computational overhead. The significance is the simplicity of the integration: the framework brings decision relevance into world-model learning without the auxiliary modules or heavy external priors described in earlier combinations. The results support treating predictive fidelity and usefulness for control as objectives that can be trained together efficiently.
icml-2026-boosting-world-models-learning.tldr: Value-Aligned World Models improve existing reinforcement-learning methods by adaptively balancing faithful dynamics modeling with task-relevant latent representations.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate reasoning through a sequence of blocks, but fixed block sizes impose a rigid structure on that process. The paper identifies two problems: different tasks can favor different block sizes, and a fixed boundary can interrupt the logical flow even within one task.

The authors observe that block-level entropy behaves differently in successful and unsuccessful reasoning. Incorrect traces show an uneven, fluctuating pattern, while correct examples exhibit a consistent downward trend. Their b1 framework uses this observation to guide reinforcement learning, training dynamic block sizes with an objective that encourages entropy to decrease monotonically as reasoning proceeds.

b1 is a post-training component designed to integrate with existing diffusion-language-model training algorithms. Across the evaluated reasoning benchmarks, it consistently improves on fixed-size block baselines. The finding supports adapting generation boundaries to the reasoning process rather than choosing one size for every task. The entropy pattern provides an empirical training signal for coherence; the abstract does not present it as a universal guarantee of correctness.
icml-2026-break-the-block-dynamic-size-r.tldr: b1 trains diffusion language models to use dynamic reasoning-block sizes, improving benchmark performance through an objective that encourages steadily decreasing entropy.

paragraphs: BRIDGE addresses a problem in extended dialogue: an agent’s visible behavior, internal representation, and stored memory can gradually diverge. Individual exchanges may remain coherent even while this inconsistency builds. A later contradiction can then undermine the persona established across many earlier turns, making consistency across these components especially important.

Before generating each response, BRIDGE jointly refines observable information, latent state, and memory toward a shared fixed point. Under the paper’s stated mild conditions, the refinement converges to a unique fixed point, providing a conditional guarantee of internal self-consistency. A separate Lyapunov-style bound addresses drift under tiered memory updates, supporting bounded persona evolution over extended interactions.

The reported evaluations place BRIDGE highest on PersonaGym and CoSER, with average scores of 4.59 and 59.5%, respectively. Gains are concentrated in persona-related measurements, including an 8.0 improvement in Character Fidelity over Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. These results are achieved while training only 0.85% of parameters with the backbone frozen, suggesting that targeted coordination of state and memory can improve persona consistency efficiently.
icml-2026-bridge-triangular-fixed-point-.tldr: BRIDGE improves long-dialogue persona consistency by refining observable information, internal state, and memory together before each response.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement-learning agents can lose coordination when an adversary replaces their actions at only a few moments. Under a strict attack budget, the challenge is identifying which interventions expose the most consequential weaknesses. The paper argues that existing attacks can miss those weaknesses while also making adversarial training expensive.

Budgeted Hierarchical Efficient Attack, or BHEA, separates the attack into distinct decisions. One part decides when to intervene and which agents to hijack; another chooses the replacement actions. This hierarchy gives the attack a structured way to allocate scarce intervention opportunities while searching for failures in the team’s coordinated behavior.

Experiments on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge show stronger attacks under the same budget. Training cooperative policies against BHEA also substantially improves robustness to limited-step action hijacking and reduces training overhead. The approach therefore serves two connected purposes: revealing coordination weaknesses more effectively and supplying adversarial experience that helps policies withstand this form of disruption. The stated robustness improvements concern the budgeted action-hijacking setting studied in the paper.
icml-2026-budget-efficient-attacks-and-r.tldr: BHEA makes limited-budget attacks on cooperative agents more effective and improves robustness when used for adversarial training.

paragraphs: This paper supplies convergence guarantees for Lion and several variants, explaining how their theoretical rates depend on problem dimension, iteration count, and distributed resources. For the original optimizer, the rate is O(d^(1/2) T^(-1/4)), where d is dimension and T is the number of iterations.

A variance-reduced variant improves the iteration dependence to T^(-1/3), retaining the same dimensional factor under an average smoothness assumption. The analysis then extends both methods to distributed training. With n nodes, their rates replace T with nT, establishing the stated linear speedup with respect to node count in these convergence bounds.

The authors also analyze a communication-efficient version that sends sign-compressed information in both directions. Using unbiased sign operations yields a bound with separate dependencies on dimension, iterations, and node count; variance reduction improves it to O(d^(1/4) T^(-1/4)). Numerical experiments support the proposed methods. Together, the results clarify how variance reduction, parallel computation, and compressed communication affect Lion’s optimization guarantees, with the stronger variance-reduced result explicitly tied to its additional smoothness assumption.
icml-2026-convergence-analysis-of-the-li.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates for Lion and shows how variance reduction, distributed computation, and sign compression change those guarantees.

paragraphs: DecoVer addresses the precision needed when language models plan tasks for embodied agents. A plan must connect actions to their conditions and consequences, and missing a step or breaking a causal relationship can make it unusable. The paper identifies these problems in approaches that generate an entire BC+ program in one attempt.

The framework combines language-model capabilities with the formal action language BC+. It first decomposes complex knowledge into hierarchical subspaces through a cascading process. It then applies two forms of verification: one checks syntactic correctness, and the other checks whether the resulting representation is executable. This gives program construction explicit structure and correctness checks.

Across the reported experiments, DecoVer outperforms language-model baselines on most evaluation metrics. The abstract reports a 12.9% success-rate gain over Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and a 60.9% improvement over GPT-5.1 on logically complex cases. These findings support decomposition and verification as useful components for translating broad language-model knowledge into more dependable embodied plans, particularly where sequential completeness and causal consistency matter.
icml-2026-decover-a-decompose-and-verify.tldr: DecoVer improves embodied task planning by decomposing BC+ knowledge representations and verifying both their syntax and executability.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks support event-driven computation, but transformer attention can introduce dense calculations and costly communication that complicate deployment on neuromorphic hardware. This paper proposes Simplified Spiking Attention and Ultra-Simplified Spiking Attention to reduce those burdens while retaining useful attention behavior for classification.

Both mechanisms substitute elementwise Hadamard products for matrix multiplication and remove components such as multiple attention heads and scaling. The analysis also finds consecutive masking redundant and examines how spike timing affects attention: earlier spikes contribute more temporal information to its modulation. These observations help motivate simplifications specific to spiking computation.

SSA changes computational complexity from O(N²D) to O(ND) and communication complexity from O(N²) to O(ND). USSA further lowers communication complexity to O(N), with only marginal reported accuracy degradation. SSA reaches 96.38%, 79.45%, and 97.56% accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and DVS-Gesture. On ImageNet-1K, SSA and USSA achieve 76.91% and 77.27%, respectively. The results demonstrate that substantial attention simplification can coexist with strong classification performance, including on the larger benchmark.
icml-2026-efficient-transformer-attentio.tldr: SSA and USSA simplify spiking-transformer attention to reduce computation and communication while maintaining strong image-classification results.

paragraphs: SPECTRA targets two observed problems in language-model training: optimizer updates can have large spectral norms, and gradient noise can contain a few unusually dominant singular values. These describe strong concentrations in the matrix structure of updates or gradients. Standard adaptive optimizers such as AdamW do not directly account for that structure.

The framework clips updates after optimization to constrain their spectral norm. It can also clip gradients beforehand to suppress sparse spectral noise spikes. The authors prove that the update-clipping step corresponds to a Composite Frank-Wolfe method with spectral constraints and weight regularization. They implement efficient soft clipping through Newton-Schulz iterations, avoiding an expensive singular value decomposition.

In language-model pretraining experiments, SPECTRA improves validation loss across the tested optimizers, including AdamW, Signum, Mars, and AdEMAMix. The strongest variants achieve the reported state-of-the-art results. Trained models also have smaller weight norms, supporting the connection between clipping and regularization. The findings position spectral clipping as a broadly applicable modification to existing optimizers in the evaluated training settings.
icml-2026-enhancing-llm-training-via-spe.tldr: SPECTRA improves language-model pretraining by clipping the spectral structure of optimizer updates and, optionally, noisy gradients.

paragraphs: Model merging combines language models through choices made in parameter space. Evolutionary search can automate those choices, but conventional search operators are stochastic and handcrafted. EvoGM aims to learn which merging coefficients tend to produce strong models, using the performance information accumulated during the search itself.

The framework uses two generators with cycle-consistent learning to propose and refine promising coefficient candidates. Historical search trajectories supply winner–loser pairs, allowing the generators to learn from relative candidate quality. This makes earlier evaluations useful training evidence for subsequent search, rather than leaving the selection of new candidates entirely to fixed heuristics.

EvoGM embeds this learned proposal process within multiple evolutionary rounds. Strong merged models become expert foundations for later rounds, so the search can build on its own successes. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, with robust performance on both seen and unseen tasks. The contribution is a learned search mechanism for model composition: the merging process uses trained generators even though the underlying motivation is composition without conventional model retraining.
icml-2026-evogm-learning-to-merge-llms-v.tldr: EvoGM learns to propose better model-merging coefficients from previous search outcomes and improves performance across seen and unseen tasks.

paragraphs: GFMate adapts graph foundation models to target domains through prompt tuning. The paper identifies a transfer problem in existing approaches: prompts can become tied to source-domain information or a particular pretraining strategy. Adaptation also commonly relies on a few labeled examples while leaving unlabeled target test data unused.

The framework introduces centroid and layer prompts after pretraining, applying them on the target domain. This placement avoids embedding the prompts into a specific source-domain pretraining procedure. A complementary learning objective then uses both labeled and unlabeled target data to tune the prompts at test time, drawing on information available where the model will operate.

Experiments across 12 benchmark datasets report superior performance and efficiency, with improvements reaching up to 30.63%. That figure represents the upper end of the reported improvements, rather than an average across datasets. The results support combining pretraining-independent prompts with adaptation to target test data, addressing both the portability of graph prompts and their ability to use information beyond the small labeled adaptation set.
icml-2026-gfmate-empowering-graph-founda.tldr: GFMate improves graph foundation models with prompts applied after pretraining and tuned using labeled and unlabeled target-domain data.

paragraphs: This paper uses sparse autoencoders to make text embeddings easier to interpret and control. Their embedding dimensions correspond to recognizable concepts, giving analysts a way to inspect what distinguishes documents and choose which properties matter. The approach addresses the expense of language-model annotation and the limited control offered by dense embeddings.

The authors study four analysis tasks: discovering semantic differences between datasets, finding unexpected concept correlations, clustering along selected properties, and retrieving documents by those properties. Filtering concepts provides direct control over clustering and retrieval. In comparisons between model responses, the method finds that Grok-4 clarifies ambiguities more often than nine other frontier models.

Across the reported tasks, SAE embeddings uncover larger differences at two to eight times lower cost than language-model methods and identify biases more reliably. They also outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval. Case studies examine changes in OpenAI model behavior and phrases Tulu-3 learned from training data. Together, these results show how interpretable representations can connect analysis of model behavior to the contents and structure of data.
icml-2026-interpretable-embeddings-with-.tldr: Sparse-autoencoder embeddings make text analysis more interpretable and controllable while improving cost and reliability in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: KineFlow forecasts time series while accounting for both uncertainty and inertia. The paper argues that pointwise regression oversmooths predictions and misses stochastic volatility. First-order generative flow methods address some of that problem, but their omission of inertia creates ambiguity in phase space and leaves them sensitive to noise.

The proposed framework introduces a neural acceleration field into flow matching. External inputs act as driving forces that gradually change momentum, rather than abruptly perturbing the state. This second-order formulation produces predictions through double integration, which the authors describe as a structural filter that suppresses high-frequency noise and promotes physically consistent behavior.

Across six real-world benchmarks, KineFlow reports an average 15% improvement in mean squared error over discriminative baselines and an 8% gain in CRPS over state-of-the-art generative methods. These comparisons address both forecasting error and the quality of probabilistic predictions. The results support modeling how motion changes over time as a useful structural choice for generative forecasting, alongside representing the uncertainty of future outcomes.
icml-2026-kineflow-kinematic-second-orde.tldr: KineFlow adds acceleration and momentum to generative time-series forecasting, improving reported prediction accuracy and probabilistic forecast quality.

paragraphs: Ophiuchus addresses medical-image tasks that require repeatedly inspecting specific visual regions while reasoning. The paper argues that generating a textual reasoning sequence is insufficient for this kind of fine-grained interaction. Its framework equips a multimodal model to decide when it needs more visual evidence and where to examine the image.

The model incorporates relevant sub-images into an interleaved visual and textual reasoning process, connecting its own grounding abilities with external tools. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning establishes basic tool selection, self-reflection fine-tuning develops decision revision, and agentic tool reinforcement learning encourages more sophisticated diagnostic behavior. These stages jointly train evidence gathering and its use in reasoning.

Evaluations report consistent improvements over both open-source and closed-source state-of-the-art methods across medical benchmarks. The tasks include visual question answering, detection, and segmentation that requires reasoning. The findings support integrating targeted visual inspection into the reasoning process for these benchmark tasks, with segmentation, understanding, and diagnostic reasoning handled within one tool-augmented framework.
icml-2026-ophiuchus-incentivizing-tool-a.tldr: Ophiuchus trains medical multimodal models to gather and revisit targeted visual evidence with tools, improving results across several medical-image benchmarks.

paragraphs: OvisOCR converts a full document-page image directly into structured Markdown. Its compact multimodal model handles this in one end-to-end process, without slicing the page into local crops or depending on separate layout detection. This design addresses the complexity and error propagation associated with pipelines that crop, recognize, and merge page regions.

Training combines detailed recognition with semantic correction. Strong OCR engines provide initial supervision, and general-model-based cleaning refines that data. Category-specific rewards then address the different demands of dense text, tables, and formulas. These rewards are designed to resolve optimization conflicts so that better structural parsing does not require sacrificing fine textual details.

On OmniDocBench, OvisOCR reports top-tier performance across all evaluated aspects among the compared methods, surpassing specialized and general approaches. The empirical results also support eliminating the error propagation associated with split-and-merge architectures. The contribution shows that a compact model can absorb capabilities supplied by elaborate training supervision and deliver them through a streamlined document-parsing process at inference.
icml-2026-ovisocr-end-to-end-document-pa.tldr: OvisOCR turns full-page images directly into Markdown with a compact model that jointly learns detailed recognition, semantic correction, and document structure.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether language models benefit from first learning abstract structure before training on richer semantic material. It uses procedural data generated by formal languages and simple algorithms as an initial warm-up. The central idea is that a small amount of structured practice can prepare a model for subsequent learning.

The authors first test which algorithmic skills different procedural datasets improve. Training on balanced-bracket sequences raises context-recall accuracy from 10% to 98% in the reported experiment. For models up to 1.3 billion parameters, placing just 0.1–0.3% procedural data at the beginning improves later pretraining on natural language, code, and informal mathematics.

The models reach comparable loss using 55%, 67%, and 86% of the original data in the respective settings, with comparable reductions in computation. Analysis finds structure introduced into both attention and MLP layers, with attention especially important for structured domains and MLP layers for language. These findings suggest that early acquisition of abstract processing skills can make later knowledge acquisition more efficient.
icml-2026-procedural-pretraining-warming.tldr: A small initial dose of procedurally generated abstract data improves later language-model pretraining and reduces the data needed to reach comparable loss.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to shrink a graph while approximately preserving triangle counts across every cut, meaning every partition of its vertices into two sides. Triangles represent higher-order structure useful for clustering and network analysis. Preserving their behavior across cuts lets a smaller representation retain this information about the original graph.

The main technical ingredient is a quantum algorithm for listing triangles. It combines a heavy–light partition of vertices with quantum walks and Grover search. Its running-time bound takes the best of three expressions involving the numbers of vertices, edges, and triangles, improving on the best known classical bounds across a broad parameter range.

Using that listing procedure, the authors construct triangle-cut sparsifiers of size approximately n/ε², up to logarithmic factors. Construction time combines triangle listing with an additional term approximately √(mn)/ε. They also prove a size lower bound of Ω(n/ε²), so the size guarantee matches it up to logarithmic factors. Applications to triangle-based clustering connect these theoretical results to graph-analysis methods that depend on higher-order relationships.
icml-2026-quantum-algorithms-for-triangl.tldr: Quantum triangle-listing algorithms enable compact triangle-cut sparsifiers with size guarantees matching a proved lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: SCoA tackles object detection when training data come from one source domain but deployment involves unseen domains. The paper argues that adapting a vision foundation model with one fixed set of style-independent parameters overlooks an important difference: distinct visual styles can create distinct mismatches for the detection task.

Its Spectral Style Modeling component uses memory to preserve local style cues and characterize varied styles within the source domain. Those signals guide a Mixture-of-Tokens Adaptation mechanism, which maintains multiple adaptation tokens and routes each sample to an appropriate combination. A third component refines object queries with style information, extending the adaptation into the detection head.

Together, these components let the detector adjust its adaptation according to the style of each sample. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across two challenging scenarios. The results support using style as an explicit conditioning signal throughout detection, from the adaptation tokens to the object queries, when learning from a single source domain and seeking generalization to domains absent from training.
icml-2026-scoa-revisiting-domain-general.tldr: SCoA conditions detector adaptation and object queries on visual style to improve generalization from one training domain to unseen domains.

paragraphs: Localized Spatial Conformal Prediction estimates uncertainty at spatial locations where observations are unavailable. Spatial data create a challenge because locations can have different local behavior and dependent observations, without the natural sequence found in time series. The paper develops conformal prediction specifically around these spatial features.

LSCP combines local quantile regression with conformal calibration and can work with different underlying prediction models. Conditioning on spatial neighborhoods allows its intervals to reflect local heterogeneity. Its guarantees depend on distinct assumptions: spatial exchangeability gives finite-sample marginal coverage, while stationarity and spatial mixing give asymptotic conditional coverage. The latter concerns increasingly large samples under the stated spatial dependence conditions.

On synthetic and real datasets, LSCP achieves coverage close to the intended level while producing tighter and more stable intervals than methods that fail to capture those dependencies. This matters because useful uncertainty estimates must balance coverage with precision. The contribution combines practical local adaptation with theoretical guarantees that explicitly distinguish overall finite-sample coverage from conditional coverage obtained asymptotically.
icml-2026-spatial-conformal-inference-th.tldr: LSCP combines neighborhood-aware quantile regression and conformal calibration to produce tighter spatial prediction intervals with assumption-dependent coverage guarantees.

paragraphs: StructMamPose estimates three-dimensional human pose from a single camera view. The paper identifies two difficulties for Mamba-based approaches: flattening structured pose information into a sequence can confuse internal state updates, and a single view makes depth difficult to infer. Both problems interfere with modeling the body’s spatial and temporal relationships.

The Identity Anchoring Mechanism introduces spatial and temporal identities into the network that generates state-update parameters. This anchors which information the model selects, suppressing spurious connections and encouraging propagation along valid structural relationships. The mechanism therefore ties sequential processing more directly to the organization of the pose data.

The View Transformation Hub addresses depth through internal coordinate rotations that expose depth-related information as planar features. This supplies explicit spatial understanding and multiple-view constraints within the model’s representation. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated datasets. Together, the two components support the paper’s shift toward structural reasoning: state updates respect meaningful relationships, while transformed internal views help organize the depth information needed for three-dimensional pose estimation.
icml-2026-structmampose-from-sequential-.tldr: StructMamPose improves monocular 3D pose estimation by anchoring state updates to pose structure and using internal coordinate rotations to support depth reasoning.

paragraphs: Thought-Aligner intervenes between an agent’s intermediate reasoning and its next action. The paper’s motivation is that small deviations in a thought can influence later tool use and propagate into unsafe behavior. Checking only the final output can therefore miss the point where a consequential action is being selected.

The method uses a separate safety model to correct unsafe thoughts before execution, then feeds the corrected version back into the agent. It leaves the underlying agent unchanged and is designed to work across agent frameworks. Training uses two-stage contrastive learning on paired safe and unsafe thoughts drawn from ten risk scenarios.

Across agent-safety benchmarks and six language models, average behavioral safety rises from about 50% without protection to around 90%. The paper reports roughly 23% better safety than state-of-the-art guardrails, alongside about a 5% improvement in helpfulness. Low per-step latency and minimal overhead support practical integration. These results show that intervening in the reasoning that guides actions can improve both safety and usefulness in the evaluated agent settings.
icml-2026-think-twice-before-you-act-enh.tldr: Thought-Aligner corrects unsafe intermediate thoughts before agents act, substantially improving reported behavioral safety while also increasing helpfulness.

paragraphs: Multi-output Gaussian processes model several related quantities together, allowing their predictions to reflect relationships between outputs. Scaling them to very large output spaces is difficult. Existing methods often simplify those relationships through low-rank or separable kernel assumptions, which can make computation manageable at the expense of expressiveness.

T-LVMOGP builds a flexible deep kernel by combining inputs with latent variables specific to each output. A Lipschitz-regularized neural network maps this information into an embedding space, where the model constructs its multi-output relationships. Stochastic variational inference supplies the scalable learning procedure. Together, these choices aim to preserve meaningful dependencies while handling many outputs.

The evaluations include climate modeling with more than 10,000 outputs and spatial transcriptomics data containing many zeros. Across the reported benchmarks, T-LVMOGP outperforms baselines in predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. The findings support learned transformations of output-specific latent representations as a way to scale probabilistic models without relying on the restrictive kernel structures identified as a bottleneck in earlier approaches.
icml-2026-transformed-latent-variable-mu.tldr: T-LVMOGP uses learned latent-variable transformations and variational inference to model thousands of correlated outputs accurately and efficiently.

paragraphs: VIAR generates images through next-scale prediction, addressing the fixed computation and high-resolution memory demands of explicit deep transformer stacks. It places an implicit equilibrium layer between shallow processing blocks. That layer reaches its representation through repeated refinement, making the number of iterations at each scale an adjustable inference setting.

Training uses Jacobian-Free Backpropagation, giving the implicit layer constant training memory. At inference, the iteration setting changes computation without retraining. On ImageNet at 256 × 256 resolution, VIAR reports FID 2.16 and sFID 8.07 using 38.4% as many parameters as VAR, matching or surpassing strong autoregressive baselines and remaining competitive with large diffusion models.

Adjusting per-scale computation reduces reported peak memory from 19.24 GB to 8.53 GB and raises throughput from 15.16 to 32.08 images per second on one RTX 4090. Ablations show convergence with few iterations and favorable quality–efficiency operating points relative to VAR. Zero-shot inpainting and class-conditional editing also show sharper details and smoother boundaries while preserving global structure, supporting the practical value of adjustable equilibrium computation.
icml-2026-visual-implicit-autoregressive.tldr: VIAR uses an implicit equilibrium layer to deliver competitive image generation with fewer parameters and adjustable inference computation without retraining.

paragraphs: XSkill helps multimodal agents improve from previous activity without updating model parameters. It distinguishes two reusable forms of knowledge: experiences that guide individual decisions and tool choices, and skills that organize planning and tool use across a task. This distinction addresses both inefficient actions and inflexible overall orchestration.

During accumulation, the framework summarizes multiple execution paths and critiques them across rollouts, grounding the resulting experiences and skills in visual observations. During inference, it retrieves and adapts that knowledge to the current visual context. Usage history then feeds back into accumulation, creating a continuing cycle of extracting, applying, and refining reusable guidance.

Evaluations span five benchmarks across diverse domains and four backbone models. XSkill consistently and substantially outperforms tool-only and learning-based baselines, with further analysis showing complementary effects from its two knowledge streams and superior zero-shot generalization. The findings support organizing past behavior at both action and task levels, while using visual context to connect stored guidance to the situation the agent currently faces.
icml-2026-xskill-continual-learning-from.tldr: XSkill improves multimodal agents without parameter updates by continually extracting and reusing visually grounded action-level experiences and task-level skills.
